source: Nersessian (2025) How do scientists think? Contributions toward a cognitive science of science (Topics in Cognitive Science)
finding: Nersessian restates the cognitive-historical method: mine archival records of historical science plus long ethnography of live labs to find how scientists reason. Her core claim is that analogy, visualisation and mental simulation work together as one process called model-based reasoning.
numbers: Ethnographic data from bioengineering labs were collected over 5 years (observation, open and semi-structured interviews, archival papers, wiki, whiteboards). Method named 'cognitive-historical' in Nersessian 1987.
limits: Self-report of her own program, not an independent test. No effect sizes or counts of cases in this paper; the Maxwell evidence is one case read from texts.
agent_relevance: O6 and O7 should be written as a linked cycle (build analogy, run it as a simulation, test it) rather than two separate tools.

source: Nersessian (2025) How do scientists think? Contributions toward a cognitive science of science (Topics in Cognitive Science)
finding: Generality of the cognitive-historical findings is argued by bootstrapping (hypotheses refined against more cases), explicitly not by inductive generalisation from cases.
numbers: No sample counts. Cases cited: Newton moon-projectile, Faraday, Maxwell, plus the bioengineering lab cases.
quote: generality is produced in a bootstrapping method commonly used in the sciences
limits: Admitted that case results are not claims about frequency in all science. Weakest point for any 'X% of discoveries used analogy' statement.
agent_relevance: Do not put base rates ('analogy precedes breakthroughs in most cases') into the schema from this literature; O6/O7 placement is a design choice.

source: Nersessian (2025) How do scientists think? Contributions toward a cognitive science of science (Topics in Cognitive Science)
finding: Nersessian says lab experiments and AI discovery programs (Klahr and Simon 1999 is named) have low ecological validity because they leave out material, social and cultural resources and the work of formulating the problem.
numbers: Names Klahr & Simon 1999 (Psychological Bulletin 125:524-543) as the contrast; no numbers.
limits: This is the rival-camp critique stated by one side. The discriminating in vitro vs in vivo comparison is in Klahr & Simon, not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Supports building O6/O7 around external artefacts (diagrams, runnable models, code checks), not pure thought.

source: Nersessian (2025) How do scientists think? Contributions toward a cognitive science of science (Topics in Cognitive Science)
finding: Structural analogies (Maxwell) are productive when relational structure maps; behavioural or functional analogies (an in vitro artery model) are productive when the model reproduces the target behaviour. So the success test differs by analogy type.
numbers: No counts. Abstraction defined broadly: idealisation, approximation, simplification, omission, limiting case, generic modelling.
limits: Typology is the author's; not tested against a rival typology.
agent_relevance: The O7 mapping check should be typed: relational mapping for structural analogies, behaviour-matching run for functional ones.

source: Clement (2022) Multiple levels of heuristic reasoning processes in scientific model construction (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Consolidates 24 heuristic processes from three books (two historians' cases in genetics and electromagnetism, plus Clement's expert think-aloud study in mechanics). Proposes a 4-level hierarchy with a Generation-Evaluation-Modification (GEM) cycle at the model-building level. Most processes are field-general; all are heuristics that may fail.
numbers: 24 processes, 3 source books, 4 hierarchy levels. Think-aloud protocols with gestures used as evidence of imagistic reasoning.
limits: Qualitative case studies with small N; the author says they suit early-stage theory building, not frequency claims. The hierarchy is a proposal, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: GEM cycle is a ready pattern for O6/O7: generate a model, evaluate it, modify it, repeat; expect many failed rounds.

source: Clement (2022) Multiple levels of heuristic reasoning processes in scientific model construction
finding: Reads Maxwell as: imagine the magnetic field as a fluid with vortices (analogy), apply a continuum-mechanics schema to get first maths, then evaluate and modify. Nersessian finds parallels between Maxwell and processes in modern expert think-aloud protocols (Clement 2008).
numbers: Convergence claim between one historical case and the Clement 2008 protocols; no statistics given.
limits: Convergence rests on interpretation by the same research tradition. No independent coder agreement in the text read.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete trace shape for a Maxwell-style run: analogy, then schema import, then qualitative check, then maths.

source: Jaeger (2026) Complementarity as Relativity: Bohr's Relativistic Analogy
finding: A recent analysis of a historical scientific analogy lists matched elements and then the dissimilarities. Bohr's analogy between quantum complementarity and relativity is weakened because quantum value determination needs an uncontrollable measurement interaction while relativistic determination does not.
numbers: One case; qualitative element-by-element comparison.
limits: Philosophy of physics paper, not a cognitive test; shows a famous analogy can be partly wrong while still useful.
agent_relevance: Strong example for O7: after mapping, list the breaks in the mapping explicitly before relying on the analogy.

source: Kretz & Krawczyk (2014) Expert analogy use in a naturalistic setting (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Recorded five weekly economics reading-group sessions and coded every analogy. Analogies were frequent; most had no surface similarity to their target.
numbers: About 7 hours recorded; 114 candidate passages (16.29 per hour); 91 confirmed, 97 analogies after splitting; coder agreement 96% on identification (kappa 0.85). Depth: 69 of 88 (78%) no surface overlap, 19 (22%) surface overlap.
limits: One group of economists, discussing others' papers (not discovery). Coding by humans, kappa 0.71 to 0.85.
agent_relevance: Expert analogy is common in talk, but this is not proof that it drives discovery.

source: Kretz & Krawczyk (2014) Expert analogy use in a naturalistic setting (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Distance was almost evenly split between within-domain and outside-domain analogies. Purpose was mostly giving an example, or making a picture.
numbers: Distance: 44 within (53%) vs 39 outside (47%) of 83. Purpose of 77: example 27 (35%), visualisation 19 (25%), exaggeration 11 (14%), inclusion 9 (12%), differentiation 8 (10%), abstraction 2 (3%), critique 1 (1%).
limits: Goal was explaining others' experiments, so purposes differ from lab problem solving.
agent_relevance: Analogies in expert talk mostly explain and rarely generate hypotheses; do not assume a far-analogy step fires often in real expert work.

source: Kretz & Krawczyk (2014) Expert analogy use in a naturalistic setting (Frontiers in Psychology) (summary of earlier in vivo studies)
finding: A review passage lists base rates from earlier real-world analogy studies; they change with setting and audience. The source studies were not opened.
numbers: Dunbar 1995/1997 and Blanchette & Dunbar: over half of biology-lab and political analogies had no surface similarity. Saner & Schunn 1999: over 75% of psychology-lab analogies within domain. Blanchette & Dunbar 2001: 77% of political-article analogies outside category. Christensen & Schunn 2007 engineering design: 55% within, 45% outside. Bearman et al. 2007 management: 73% structural only.
limits: Secondhand figures as reported by Kretz & Krawczyk; originals not opened (search quota ran out). Coding schemes differ across studies.
agent_relevance: Far analogies come mainly with general audiences; experts talking to experts use near ones. Matches placing far analogues at impasses only.

source: Kretz & Krawczyk (2014) Expert analogy use in a naturalistic setting (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Partial non-replication of Christensen & Schunn's idea that within-domain analogies carry more surface similarity than distant ones: no such constraint among the economists.
numbers: Structural analogies split 31 outside / 31 within; superficial analogies 7 outside / 6 within.
limits: Small counts (13 superficial analogies); different discipline and goals.
agent_relevance: Distance alone is a weak predictor of whether a source is deep; use a mapping check, not distance, to judge quality.

source: Richland & Zhao (2026) Relational Reasoning and Educational Applications (review)
finding: Teaching-by-comparison work shows relational transfer rises when the correspondences are made visible. Richland & McDonough (2010) high-cuing conditions gave more extension to new contexts and less capture by misleading surface features, immediately and one week later.
numbers: Two experiments with college students learning permutation and combination from controlled videos. Effect sizes not given in the review text.
limits: Secondhand; lab videos on mathematics, not discovery. The review also cites the Alfieri, Nokes-Malach & Schunn 2013 meta-analysis of case comparison (figures not in the text read).
agent_relevance: Cue the mapping explicitly (align parts side by side) when O7 is used, rather than hoping the model finds it.

source: Richland & Zhao (2026) Relational Reasoning and Educational Applications (review)
finding: Relational attention is trainable. Adults primed by generating far-distance analogies attended more to relations on a later scene-analogy task. Among 272 elementary pupils, latent class analysis found four relational-attention clusters linked to classroom maths learning.
numbers: Vendetti et al. 2014 and Walker et al. 2018 (adult priming); Simms & Richland 2019 (3 to 4 year olds, self-generated relations beat passive listening); Zhao et al. 2025a N=272, 4 clusters.
limits: Priming effect sizes not in the text read; transfer to scientific discovery is not shown.
agent_relevance: A cheap warm-up (state the relations in the current problem before retrieval) is a plausible O7 precondition; needs testing on the agent.

source: Richland & Zhao (2026) Relational Reasoning and Educational Applications (review)
finding: Reports that expert geoscientists spontaneously generate analogies grounded in causal principles (Goldwater, Gentner et al. 2021), consistent with experts attending to relational structure.
numbers: No figures in the passage read.
limits: Secondhand; the Goldwater paper itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Expert advantage is in which relation is noticed, which a prompt can mimic by asking for causal structure first.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Nat Hum Behav)
finding: GPT-3 beat the average undergraduate on a new text-only Raven-style task and matched or beat humans on verbal analogies.
numbers: Digit Matrices vs humans (N=40): generative odds ratio 1.88, p=0.005, CI 1.21 to 2.91; multiple choice OR 6.27, p=2.3e-8, CI 3.28 to 11.99. Best human scored 100%. On SAT analogies GPT-3 exceeded the estimated high-school average; on the Jones et al. set it was in range but numerically lower.
limits: Tasks may be in training data (disputed by Hodel & West, Lewis & Mitchell). Digit Matrices differ from visual Raven items.
agent_relevance: Base models can do simple analogy; this says nothing yet about distant, scientific analogy.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Nat Hum Behav)
finding: On story analogies that need higher-order causal relations, GPT-3 was weaker than students, especially for far (cross-domain) analogies.
numbers: Humans N=54: t(53)=21.3 vs chance; 15 of 54 right on every trial. GPT-3 near: p=0.0039; far: p=0.065 (not significant). GPT-3 vs humans OR=0.37, p=0.0003. GPT-4 in an initial check did better (no figures given).
limits: GPT-3 only in this paper.
agent_relevance: The far-analogy gap is the case O7 cares about; do not trust unaided far mapping.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Re-ran Webb's letter-string tasks with permuted alphabets and symbol alphabets. Humans held up; GPT models dropped sharply. A comprehension check showed the models understood the permuted order, so the failure is not simple misreading.
numbers: 136 Prolific participants. Overall accuracy (Table 2; 1,876 human and 6,840 per-model samples): humans 0.753 [0.734,0.773]; the three GPT models 0.488, 0.350, 0.452 in the order printed (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 likely; column labels garbled in PDF text). Comprehension check mostly 0.9 to 1.0.
limits: Prompt follows Hodel & West; the counting-bottleneck explanation was later argued by Webb et al. 2024. Human pool differs from Webb's (this one scored higher).
agent_relevance: A failed generality test: familiar analogies pass, re-coded ones fail. Test O7 on re-coded versions.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were no better than GPT-3 on these problems; GPT-3.5 often applied an alternate rule.
numbers: Error share from alternate rules: GPT-3 5.81%, GPT-4 22%, GPT-3.5 38.59%; humans about 15% in a similar category.
limits: Percentages come from a table with garbled columns; read with care.
agent_relevance: Chat tuning may cost analogy skill; do not assume a newer model maps better.

source: Hodel & West (2023/2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Independent critique with new data: GPT-3 fails simple variants of the same tasks while humans stay high.
numbers: 121 UW undergraduates. GPT-3 generative accuracy under 0.1 on the synthetic alphabet for extend, successor, predecessor and fix-sequence; only remove-redundant and sort stayed near the original range. N=50 instances per condition.
limits: Single model (GPT-3); the counting explanation could apply.
agent_relevance: Strengthens the case that analogy tests need re-coded variants.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Rebuttal: GPT-4 with code execution solved the permuted-alphabet analogies at human level; the failure was in counting letter positions, not in analogy.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). GPT-4 vs humans P=8.9e-13 (humans better); GPT-4 + code vs humans P=0.496 (no difference). Of GPT-4's errors 46% used a valid alternative rule vs 39% for humans in Lewis & Mitchell.
limits: GPT-4 answers checked by hand; code use is not a human strategy; one task family.
agent_relevance: Tool use fixes a non-analogy bottleneck; give O7 a code tool for the bookkeeping parts.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring LMs through counterfactual tasks
finding: Across 11 tasks, language models stay above chance on counterfactual variants but performance drops substantially and consistently, suggesting partly narrow, non-transferable procedures.
numbers: 11 tasks; GPT-4 with 0-shot chain of thought in the headline figure. Per-task figures not read.
limits: Only the first page and abstract were read; per-task numbers not checked.
agent_relevance: Same warning as for analogy: test on re-coded forms.

source: Hu, Storks, Lewis & Chai (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Turning Raven-matrix pictures into language let models solve them zero-shot; better abstractions helped.
numbers: GPT-3 175B on RAVEN with 1, 2 or 3 rows: Center 36.8%, 69.2%, 77.2% (human 95.6%); 2x2Grid 54.0, 71.0, 78.0 (human 81.8); 3x3Grid 73.0, 85.2, 86.4 (human 79.6). Table text partly garbled.
limits: Synthetic puzzles; the authors did the perceptual encoding.
agent_relevance: Representation change (O6) before mapping (O7) raises success.

source: Hu, Storks, Lewis & Chai (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Ablations: structural decomposition raised accuracy by about 20% on average; attribute names matter. Real names beat random names by over 20 points in larger models; random values for the orientation attribute lowered Center accuracy only a few points.
numbers: Random vs RAVEN orientation values: 72.6% vs 76.0%, 77.8% vs 80.0%. 125M model accuracy doubled 22.2% to 45.6% with naming; OPT 1.3B 47.2% to 72.0%.
limits: Raven-type puzzles only.
agent_relevance: How a problem is re-described matters more than which analogy is chosen; supports O6 before O7.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Asking the model to recall its own related problems before solving beat zero-shot chain of thought and slightly beat hand-written few-shot chain of thought.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo 77.8% (vs 75.8 to 76.7 for the CoT baselines; table partly garbled); MATH 37.3% vs 33.9 to 34.9; text-davinci-003 GSM8K 61.0% vs 50.3 to 54.0. Codeforces Acc@1 15% (GPT-3.5-16k) and 19% (GPT-4) vs 8 to 11% and 16 to 17% for baselines.
limits: Gains are 1 to 3 points on strong models; 'analogy' here is self-recalled examples, not cross-domain mapping. Table cell alignment uncertain.
agent_relevance: A cheap O7 variant; do not expect big gains on routine tasks.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Boundary condition: self-generated exemplars need a capable model. Small models do better with real labelled exemplars. Using only one generated exemplar hurts.
numbers: GSM8K with GPT-3.5: K=1 76.1 vs K=3 77.5 (K=3 or 5 best); text-curie-001 and text-davinci-001 prefer few-shot with labelled examples; text-davinci-002 and 003 prefer self-generated.
limits: Only OpenAI and PaLM2 models.
agent_relevance: Gate self-analogy by model strength; use about 3 sources, not one.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind expert review found LLM research ideas more novel than human experts' ideas and a little less feasible.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition, 79 reviewers, 298 reviews. Novelty (review level): human 4.84 (n=119), AI 5.64 (n=109), AI + human rerank 5.81; idea-level AI 5.62, p=0.03. Feasibility human 6.61 vs AI 6.34 (not significant). Excitement 4.55 vs 5.19 (p=0.04).
limits: Ideas not executed; reviewer agreement only 56.1% (NeurIPS 2021 about 66%); the system is retrieval-augmented generation, not analogy as such.
agent_relevance: Novelty judged by experts can rise through retrieval-based generation; keep a feasibility check.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Failure modes: heavy duplication and unreliable LLM self-judging.
numbers: 4,000 seed ideas gave only about 200 non-duplicates (about 5%); Claude-3.5-Sonnet reached 71.4% pairwise accuracy picking accepted ICLR papers (GPT-4o 61.1%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%).
limits: Single field (NLP).
agent_relevance: Many draws of an analogy step will repeat; dedupe, and judge pairwise rather than by score.

source: Yang et al. (2024) MOOSE: LLMs for automated open-domain scientific hypotheses discovery
finding: Retrieved inspirations (the 'analogy source') changed novelty only modestly, and judging was done by GPT-4.
numbers: GPT-4 scores (validness, novelty, helpfulness): random inspirations 3.773, 2.957, 3.643; BM25 3.585, 3.364, 3.670; GPT-3.5 picked 3.812, 2.818, 3.733; ground-truth inspirations 3.876, 3.000, 3.806; ground-truth hypotheses 3.700, 3.380, 3.880. Randomised-corpus ablation: novelty 3.227 vs 3.390 for full system.
limits: GPT-4 judge may grade validity by familiarity (authors say so); small scale, social science.
agent_relevance: Smart retrieval of analogues barely beat random; checking and feedback loops matter more than source choice.

source: Wang et al. (2024) SciMON: Scientific inspiration machines optimized for novelty
finding: Literature-inspiration retrieval plus iterative novelty boosting improved ideas, but they still fell short of real papers' ideas.
numbers: Ground truth judged significantly higher in technical level and novelty in 85% of comparisons. GPT4FS+KG more technical in 48% and less incremental in 45% of pairs vs GPT4FS. Novelty iteration: 88.9% of updated ideas substantially different, 55.6% more novel; second iteration 57.8% gained.
limits: Small human annotation; novelty boosting adds generic words.
agent_relevance: Iterating against related work helps; headroom stays large.

source: Radensky et al. (2026) Scideator: human-LLM facet recombination and novelty evaluation (CAIS 2026)
finding: Splitting papers into purpose, mechanism and evaluation facets and recombining them (analogy across contexts) gave more creativity support than a baseline; facet-based retrieval carried the novelty checker.
numbers: 22 researchers, within-subjects, Wilcoxon p<.01 for creativity support. Retrieval ablation top-10 hit: full 89.66% vs 13.79, 10.34, 8.62, 5.17% for ablations. Classifier zero-shot 0.68 accuracy, 0.65 macro-F1 on 43 held-out ideas (26 novel, 17 not).
limits: Small sample; self-reported creativity scale; ablations from one system.
agent_relevance: Facet decomposition is a typed mapping the agent can use for O7.
